messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

The assault happened on a Tuesday evening in late October, just after Lena had locked up her jewelry shop. She was closing the security gate when a man she recognized from the neighborhood—someone who had come into her store twice before, looking at rings he never bought—stepped out from the alley beside her building. He grabbed her wrist, twisted it until she dropped her keys, and pressed something hard against her ribs. She remembered the smell of his jacket, damp and metallic, and the way his voice was almost gentle when he told her not to scream. What she could not remember, no matter how hard she tried, was how she got from the alley to the ground. There was a gap there, a complete blank, and then a sudden fragment: the concrete against her cheek, the sound of his footsteps running away. She had pushed the memory back so many times that it arrived now in pieces, unbidden—a flash of his hand on her arm, a wave of nausea that came from nowhere, and then nothing again.

In the weeks that followed, Lena found herself unable to shake the feeling that she was contaminated. She showered twice a day, sometimes three times, but the sensation of his grip lingered on her skin. She told herself that her reaction was proof of weakness—that a stronger person would have fought back, would have screamed, would not have frozen the way she did. This belief that she was a lousy coper became a kind of background hum, and it made the world feel more dangerous. If she could not trust herself to handle a threat, then every stranger approaching her on the sidewalk was a potential catastrophe. She began to scan for exits as soon as she entered any room—the coffee shop, the post office, even her own apartment—and she felt safe only in the narrow space behind her workbench at the shop, where she could keep her back to the wall and her eyes on the door.

The triggers were everywhere. Seeing the offender was the worst—she had spotted him once, three blocks from her shop, and her stomach had turned inside out. She had ducked into a doorway and waited, trembling, until she was sure he was gone. But even without seeing him, the nausea came when she least expected it: a customer talking about someone losing a loved one, a news report about a robbery, the smell of damp wool on a rainy day. Each time her stomach lurched, the memory fragments surged back—the pressure of his hand, the blank space in her mind—and each time, she felt more convinced that she was falling apart. The nausea itself became a signal that danger was near, and so she started watching for it, bracing herself, which only made the world feel more saturated with threat.

Her scanning for exits became automatic, but it also kept the memory alive. Every time she checked a doorway or mapped an escape route, she was reminded of the alley, of how she had not seen him coming. The threat monitoring fed the intrusions, and the intrusions fed the threat monitoring, until Lena could not tell which came first. She started avoiding the street where her shop was located, taking a longer route to work that added twenty minutes to her commute. She stopped going to the grocery store after dark. She told her friends she was too busy to meet for coffee, because the cafe had too many corners and too many strangers and she could not breathe until she was back behind her workbench, where the only things that mattered were the weight of a stone and the steady pressure of her tools.

What finally brought her to seek help was a morning in early January, when she found herself unable to unlock her shop door. She stood on the sidewalk, keys in hand, and the nausea rose so fast that she vomited into the gutter. A customer asked if she was okay, and Lena could not answer. She was certain that she was broken, that her reactions had proven she was a lousy coper, but she was also terrified that if she did not find a way out of this cycle, she would lose the only place she still felt even remotely safe. She came to therapy because she was desperate to feel clean again, and because she could no longer bear the weight of scanning every room for a threat that might never come—but that she could not stop looking for.
